title: Concerning the Going Concern
coreMove: Replace inherited informality with operating architecture that clarifies ownership and cadence.
sourcePressure: Scaling turns founder access and ad hoc alignment into coordination debt, requiring mission-linked process, stage-fit executives, escalation paths, and behavior loops.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version is adding process because the company is bigger.

hook: scaling breaks what made you special

exampleSpecs.domain: chain of urgent-care clinics expanding from three sites to twelve
exampleSpecs.audience: a founder whose site leads keep escalating staffing decisions directly to her
exampleSpecs.stakes: patient wait times and nurse turnover rise because ownership is unclear
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the founder moves staffing authority from hallway escalation to a weekly site-capacity cadence with named owners and an exception threshold
exampleSpecs.firstImage: twelve clinic schedules spread across a conference table with sticky flags

exampleSpecs.domain: robotics warehouse integrator adding enterprise customers
exampleSpecs.audience: a COO whose best early engineer is failing as a multi-team executive
exampleSpecs.stakes: installation teams wait for heroic fixes instead of predictable escalation
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the COO compares the engineer's early-stage strengths with current enterprise bottlenecks, then redesigns the role instead of honoring reputation
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a stalled robot arm beside an enterprise acceptance checklist

exampleSpecs.domain: regional seafood processor coordinating boats, plant, and distributors
exampleSpecs.audience: a general manager whose informal dock conversations no longer align the plant
exampleSpecs.stakes: fresh product spoils when catch timing and distributor pickups conflict
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager replaces dockside favors with a daily catch-to-dispatch meeting and marks one person accountable for changing pickup promises
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a crate of unsold scallops sweating beside a pickup manifest

exampleSpecs.domain: national youth soccer nonprofit adding regional directors
exampleSpecs.audience: an executive director seeing local chapters interpret values differently
exampleSpecs.stakes: scholarship access varies by region while the mission statement stays unchanged
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director chooses two behaviors to review monthly, ties grants to those behaviors, and stops treating the mission poster as culture enforcement
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a scholarship approval folder beside a rolled-up mission banner

exampleSpecs.domain: precision agriculture drone company moving from pilots to support contracts
exampleSpecs.audience: a CEO whose customer-success team lacks escalation rules for crop-season outages
exampleSpecs.stakes: farmers lose survey windows when support improvises priorities
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the CEO asks which outage gets escalated first, hears three answers, and creates a severity ladder tied to crop windows
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a drone case open beside a crop-stage calendar

exampleSpecs.domain: university research center turning into a contract lab
exampleSpecs.audience: a lab director whose academic norms clash with delivery commitments
exampleSpecs.stakes: sponsor deadlines require different review loops than grant-driven research
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director identifies one inherited academic habit that now creates decision latency and converts it into a sponsor-review gate
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a sponsor milestone chart pinned over an old grant-review calendar

skillTargets: identify when informality has become coordination debt
design process in service of mission
evaluate executive fit by company stage
spot behavior loops that actually program culture

tryThisNowSpec: Name one recurring escalation that still depends on personal access. Write the owner, cadence, and exception rule that would let the organization handle it without you.
sourceAnchorsNote: source contains no named anecdote for this chapter
